Right Lower Quadrant Pain

appendix, ileocecum, or neither · Campylobacter and Yersinia · appendix-sparing imaging · when to treat CampylobacterIs there profuse mucoid diarrhea, and is there a sick contact?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness and a neutrophil leukocytosis fit appendicitis and infectious ileocecitis alike and decide nothing. Profuse mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact points to infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis) from Campylobacter or Yersinia: supportive care, no surgery.
  • Appendicitis is periumbilical pain that settles at the McBurney point, with anorexia, vomiting and little or no diarrhea: surgical consultation, with imaging before the operation (US first in a child, CT otherwise). Clinical references treat the classic picture as a clinical diagnosis, because delaying surgery for imaging only raises the risk of perforation; the board cards image first.
  • In an adolescent girl, a pregnancy test comes first: ectopic pregnancy is often mistaken for appendicitis.

Campylobacter and Yersinia favor the ileocecum, and Yersinia also inflames the mesenteric nodes (mesenteric adenitis); imaging shows ileocecal inflammation with a normal appendix. Campylobacter can begin in the jejunum and then reach the ileum and cecum, so its pain can migrate like appendicitis. In children, appendicitis follows obstruction of the lumen, usually by lymphoid hyperplasia. Bowel movements usually slow or stop in appendicitis; when diarrhea is present, suspect a retrocecal appendix.

2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingPoints toAction
Rebound tenderness, guarding or rigidityPeritonitis from a ruptured appendixSurgical consultation now; IV fluids and a third-generation cephalosporin before appendectomy.
Adolescent girl with a positive pregnancy testWork up ectopic pregnancy before anything else.
Sudden, severe pain in a girl, usually with vomitingAdnexal (ovarian) torsionPelvic US with Doppler and immediate surgery to save the ovary.
Bloody diarrhea with little fever in a childNo antibiotics; isotonic IV fluids, which may limit kidney injury; watch for hemolytic uremic syndrome.
3Differential
Right lower quadrant pain in a young patient
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Infectious ileocecitis (pseudoappendicitis): Campylobacter, YersiniaProfuse mucoid diarrhea or a sick contact, with fever, right lower quadrant pain and leukocytosis; Campylobacter after undercooked poultry or a puppy, Yersinia after pork or unpasteurized milk, often in toddlers; puppies carry both.Supportive care; a stool culture or nucleic acid amplification test names the organism.
Acute appendicitisPeriumbilical pain moving to the McBurney point, anorexia, vomiting; little or no diarrhea, no sick contact; rebound once it ruptures.Surgical consultation and imaging (US first in a child); appendectomy.
Undercooked beef or an outbreak; bloody stool within 1 to 3 days; fever above 38.5 °C is rare.No antibiotics; watch for hemolytic uremic syndrome.
NorovirusOutbreak with prominent vomiting; watery stools that rarely contain mucus or blood; normal white blood cell count.Supportive care.
Adolescent girl with a positive pregnancy test; often mistaken for appendicitis.Order the ectopic workup before anything else (step 2).
Adnexal torsionGirl with sudden, severe pain, usually with vomiting; an enlarged ovary, and decreased or absent Doppler flow supports it.Immediate surgery to untwist the ovary.
Crohn ileitisChronic, relapsing pain, weight loss, perianal disease; the terminal ileum is its usual site.Colonoscopy with ileal intubation and biopsy.
Cecal diverticulitisRight-sided diverticular inflammation in an adult; exceedingly rare at 17; mild or no diarrhea.Exclude it by age; order the workup for the other rows.
4Workup
Treatment by cause
CauseFirst lineWhen it changes
CampylobacterSupportive care with rehydration; usually self-limited within 7 days.Beyond 7 days, bloody stools, high fever, pregnancy, immunocompromise or old age: azithromycin; with resistance, an agent the sensitivity panel shows works (amoxicillin in the source case); avoid doxycycline under age 8 when another agent covers the organism.
YersiniaSupportive care; self-limited.Septic complications: a third-generation cephalosporin, a fluoroquinolone or trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, by susceptibility.
AppendicitisIV third-generation cephalosporin, then appendectomy.Perforated: continue the antibiotic after surgery, for 4 days. Pain for 5 days or more with a contained abscess: bowel rest, IV fluids and antibiotics, then interval appendectomy at 6 to 8 weeks.
Adnexal torsionImmediate laparoscopy to untwist the ovary and try to restore its blood flow.Surgery is not delayed: suspicion alone is enough to operate.
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
A dozen mucus-laden stools in a day with fever, and a sibling or day-care contact with the same illnessInfectious ileocecitis, which appendicitis cannot explainSupportive care.
Pork, unpasteurized milk or a puppy in a toddler (a puppy fits Campylobacter too)YersiniaSupportive care.
Migratory pain with profuse diarrheaCampylobacter spreading from the jejunum to the ileocecumSupportive care; the migration alone is no reason to operate.
A susceptibility panel in a mild, improving childThe susceptibility panel is not an indicationSymptomatic care only.
Diarrhea with otherwise classic appendicitis signsA retrocecal appendixImage before setting appendicitis aside.

Pause point. The bait: the migratory pain. Fever, right lower quadrant tenderness and leukocytosis are shared; profuse diarrhea or a sick contact moves the answer to infectious ileocecitis, which needs no surgery.

Practice
  1. 17-year-old boy with 3 days of fever and cramping pain that began near the navel and settled in the right lower quadrant; a dozen mucus-laden loose stools since yesterday; his younger brother had the same illness last week → Campylobacter infection → Infectious ileocecitis
  2. 17-year-old boy on day 3 of fever and right lower quadrant pain that started near the navel, with frequent mucus-laden stools and a brother sick with the same illness; stable vital signs, no rebound, no blood in the stool → Supportive care with stool studies → Usually self-limited within 7 days
  3. 17-year-old boy with presumed Campylobacter ileocecitis returns on day 9 of illness; his stools are now bloody, his temperature is 39.5 °C, and the right lower quadrant is tender without rebound or guarding → Start antimicrobial therapy → A high-risk criterion is met
  4. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain, anorexia and vomiting but no diarrhea, with rebound tenderness → Surgical consultation for appendectomy → The classic script without the stool
  5. 17 yo with right lower quadrant pain and diarrhea in whom the diagnosis remains unclear after examination → Cross-sectional imaging of the abdomen → Ileocecal inflammation with a spared appendix
  6. 16 yo with months of right lower quadrant pain, weight loss and a perianal fistula → Colonoscopy with ileal intubation → Crohn ileitis
  7. 6 yo with severe crampy abdominal pain and grossly bloody stools, temperature 37.6 C, after a family cookout → Escherichia coli O157:H7 infection → Hematochezia early, high fever rare
  8. That 6 year old with suspected Shiga toxin producing E coli; which intervention should be withheld → Empiric antibiotics → Risk of precipitating hemolytic uremic syndrome
  9. Three weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, ascending symmetric weakness with areflexia → Guillain-Barre syndrome → The classic post-infectious sequela
  10. Two weeks after a Campylobacter enteritis, asymmetric oligoarthritis with conjunctivitis and urethritis → Reactive arthritis → The second named sequela
  11. 6-year-old girl with 5 days of mucoid diarrhea, now 4 loose stools a day; afebrile, well hydrated, no blood in the stool; culture grows Campylobacter, ciprofloxacin resistant, macrolide intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Symptomatic care only → mild and self-limited; the susceptibility panel is not an indication
  12. 6 yo with Campylobacter coli enteritis now on day 9 with bloody stools; ciprofloxacin resistant, erythromycin intermediate, ampicillin and tetracycline sensitive → Amoxicillin → sensitive, and safe under 8
  13. 4 yo in day care with high fever, bloody diarrhea and a brief generalized seizure; stool grows Shigella → Azithromycin → treating shortens illness and spread
Decoy note A contact's bloody stools can pull toward Shiga toxin E. coli in a patient whose own stool has no blood: a contact's findings describe the exposure, not this patient's illness. Migratory pain is also explained by Campylobacter spread, so it does not confirm appendicitis.
Bacterial diarrhea: who gets antibiotics Campylobacter and Yersinia: see Treatment by cause in step 4 · Shiga toxin-producing E. coli: bloody diarrhea with little fever; no antibiotics, which can raise the risk of hemolytic uremic syndrome · Shigella: high fever with mucoid, bloody diarrhea, sometimes a seizure; antibiotics such as azithromycin shorten illness and shedding · Clostridioides difficile: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin first line
Pearls Appendicitis explains neither a dozen mucoid stools nor a sick sibling; ileocecal Campylobacter or Yersinia explains both. · Profuse diarrhea or a sick contact should halt a planned appendectomy for a second look. · In pseudoappendicitis, imaging shows ileocecal inflammation and enlarged mesenteric nodes with a normal appendix. · Campylobacter can begin in the jejunum, so its pain may migrate like appendicitis. · The two tested Campylobacter sequelae are Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis.
Pairs with Acute Kidney Injury in a Child covers hemolytic uremic syndrome from the renal side, where the E. coli O157:H7 branch ends. Anemia with Thrombocytopenia covers hemolytic uremic syndrome as hemolysis with low platelets. Infectious Diarrhea covers the organism by exposure. Ask: whose stool was bloody, and how many days into the illness?
Transferable rule When a presentation fits a textbook script, look for the finding the script cannot explain, such as a symptom the disease does not produce or an exposure it cannot have.
Salient decoyAcute appendicitis is not associated with profuse watery then mucoid diarrhea and cannot explain a sibling with the same illness. There are no peritoneal signs.
True-fact-wrong-slotE. coli O157:H7 causes hematochezia in the patient within 1 to 3 days, and fever above 38.5 °C rarely occurs. Bloody stools in a contact are not this patient's.
Class-vs-memberNorovirus gives watery stools that rarely contain mucus, a normal white blood cell count, and prominent vomiting.
Unchecked attributeCecal diverticulitis is exceedingly rare at this age and does not produce profuse mucoid diarrhea.
Test-overrides-findingsA susceptibility panel invites treatment, but a mild, improving, afebrile child is treated by the clinical picture, not the culture report.
